So cornbread dressing. There are about 50 gabillion ways to do it. Everyone has their own way of making it. Basically just start out with a good cornbread recipe. You can use white cornmeal or yellow cornmeal. You can use the regular stuff or stone ground. The key is to bake it in a well seasoned cast iron skillet.

For the cornbread I do:

1 cup cornmeal 1 cup whole (do not get lowfat, etc,, must be whole) buttermilk 1 extra large egg 1/3 cup melted lard (the original recipe I got from my MIL used canola oil, lard has the same number of calories and just trust me, tastes a LOT better) 2 Tablespoons flour

Just mix it all together. It's going to be lumpy and ugly, that's OK. Take a little extra lard to coat the inside of the cast iron skillet and cook it in a preheated 400 degree oven for 30 minutes.

Cornbread dressing is basically just people taking cornbread and mashing it all up and destroying the cornbread in a huge bowl and then mixing in whatever else they want as far as canned soups, crackers, bread, etc.. My husband likes celery cornbread dressing so I get a massively huge bowl and mash and mush up the cornbread. I usually do two pans of the cornbread for this but you can triple, quadruple this if you want to and then once your dressing is made you can freeze it raw. It freezes incredibly well and actually tastes better if you do so rather than cooking it fresh.

OK, so take your mashed up cooked cornbread and add a ton of finely chopped celery and yellow (sweet) onion. I'm sorry I don't have an exact recipe because this is Southern cooking we're talking about. I will usually use one to one and half big sweet onions though and at least a whole bunch of celery if not more. I throw it in the food processor so I always get a bit of "celery juice" in there too with it.

Throw that in the bowl with the cornbread. Add about two to three cans of cream of chicken soup and salt and pepper and chicken broth, at least three to four raw eggs, and at least a sleeve of just regular plain soda crackers. We ran out of cream of chicken soup one year and it was too dry so I had to add a can of cream of mushroom. It made it taste better so I always add in at least one can of that too now!

How much of what to put in I can't tell you because I honestly just don't know. I always scrub my hands and wrists and up to my elbows really, really well because this works best if you just mush it all up with your hands and don't use a spoon. Don't ask me why. I've never seen anyone mix dressing with anything other than their hands, lol.

You don't want it too runny and you don't want it looking too dry either. The best description I can think of would be the consistency of oatmeal.

It actually tastes better if you freeze it first, then unthaw it and add a little bit of extra chicken broth. I will normally make one huge batch and freeze half for Christmas and just put the other half in the fridge to pull out and cook for Thanksgiving. The Christmas batch always tastes better, don't ask me why.

When it comes time to cook be sure to use some Crisco or butter at the bottom of your pan. The important thing to remember is to start it early because you have to preheat to around 300 degrees and make sure, make sure you put some aluminum foil over the top. Also, put it only about an inch to an inch and a half in the pan. I like it a little thicker but if you go too thick it will never cook and I learned that lesson the hard way. It has to cook long and slow for hours. If we are eating early afternoon I try to get it in the oven around 7 or 8 a.m. For the last hour of cooking you remove the foil to let the top cook and slightly brown a little. You'll know when it's done because you will just test it the same way you would a cake. Stick a knife in and if it comes out clean pull the foil off to just slightly brown the top.

I've seen people do cooked shredded chicken in their dressing or use whole chopped boiled eggs instead of raw eggs in theirs. I've even heard of people doing oyster dressing (beats me) but this is the one we do. Some people add sage (we really aren't big fans of sage).

I don't think there's really a wrong way to do it. This was how my husband's grandmother made hers and I got the recipe from my MIL after his grandmother passed. I've actually never asked my dad how he makes his because I love the celery. I think next year I am going to experiment and throw in some celery salt instead of just regular and see what that does!
